title: Honest work
hookLine: Guru Nanak squeezed two meals, and one bled: the Sikh, Muslim and Buddhist teachings on honest earning
tomorrow: a monk lay sick and alone. who finally came to wash him?

lines: MILK FROM ONE, BLOOD FROM THE OTHER.
cards: Rounding up a timesheet. Calling a stock photo your own. Small things, and nobody checks.
Sikh tradition tells a story about exactly that. Guru Nanak, the story goes, stayed in a town with Lalo, a carpenter who lived on coarse bread he earned with his own hands.
A rich official, Malik Bhago, threw a feast and demanded the Guru come. He came. Then he took Lalo's dry bread in one hand and Bhago's rich food in the other, and squeezed.
From Lalo's bread, milk. From Bhago's feast, blood. So why would bread bleed?

teach.h: WEALTH SQUEEZED OUT OF THE POOR.
teach.b: Because, the story says, Bhago's wealth had been squeezed out of the poor. The food carried how it was earned.

teach.h: KIRAT KARNI: EARN BY HONEST WORK.
teach.b: The story comes from the janamsakhis, the life stories Sikhs tell of Guru Nanak, and it sits behind a plain Sikh teaching: kirat karni, earning by honest work.
In the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says that the one who eats what he earns by his own effort, and gives some of it away, is the one who recognizes the path.
Sikh teaching sets it beside two others: remember God, and share what you have. Two neighbor traditions say it in their own words.

teach.h: FROM THE WORK OF HIS OWN HANDS.
teach.b: A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari has the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying that no one eats better food than what he eats from the work of his own hands.
And the Buddha's eightfold path includes right livelihood: earning in a way that does no harm. Three traditions, each with its own reasons. The puzzle's answer isn't a magic trick.

It's a question about a paycheck: what got squeezed into it? Lalo's bread wasn't holy because it was plain. It was clean because nothing in it was taken: not someone else's time, not their credit, not their sweat.

how: Sikhs speak of kirat karni, earning by honest work, alongside remembering God and sharing; Muslims and Buddhists have their own teachings on honest earning and right livelihood.

o: working longer hours than everyone else on the team
earning in a way you could show anyone, start to finish
a job that pays well enough to live on comfortably

games.q: bread, milk and blood: tap the pairs.
p: a carpenter with coarse, honest bread
a rich official with a feast
earning in a way that does no harm

s: the Lalo story is written in the Guru Granth Sahib
it comes from the janamsakhis, the life stories of Guru Nanak. the scripture gives the teaching.
a hadith praises eating from the work of your own hands
Sahih al-Bukhari records it: no one eats better food than that.
honest work is only about big money, like Bhago's feast
Lalo's bread was small. the story is about how it was earned.

games.q: a client asks if the photos in your pitch are your own. some are licensed stock. what would kirat karni ask of you?
o: say which ones are stock; the work should be what it claims to be.
say yes; they look original, and the client will never check.
change the subject; dodging the question isn't technically lying.
games.why: honest work means what you hand over is what you say it is. the feast bled because of how it was gotten.

practice: Pick up one thing your work paid for: your phone, your lunch, the cup in front of you. Hold it, and ask Lalo's question quietly: how was this earned?
If one part of your work wouldn't survive being squeezed, just name it to yourself, and keep breathing.

wordCard.voice: Honest work: earning by your own effort, so the bread holds milk, not blood. Sikhs call it kirat karni.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: doing honest work. a core Sikh teaching.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: honest, like Lalo's bread, coarse and clean all the way through. See you tomorrow.
